slides.headline: This small seabird flies 70,900 km every year.
slides.sub: The Arctic tern weighs under 125 g and goes from the Arctic to Antarctica and back

slides.label: km a year, the average for 11 tracked terns
slides.body: Individual birds ranged from 59,500 to 81,600 km. The figure leaves out their flights during the breeding season.

slides.headline: Pole to pole and back
slides.body: Terns tagged in Greenland and Iceland flew to Antarctic waters. The study called it the longest round-trip animal migration ever recorded electronically.

slides.headline: Slow going south, fast coming back
slides.body: The trip south took about 93 days, with a stop of about 25 days in the North Atlantic. The return took about 40.

slides.label: km a day, the average on the way back north
slides.body: The daily range was 390–670 km, from Antarctica to south Greenland.

slides.headline: Three trips to the Moon
slides.body: Arctic terns can live more than 30 years. A lifetime total may exceed 2.4 million km, about three return journeys to the Moon.

slides.headline: Send this to someone who dreads long flights.
slides.body: Big numbers, taken straight from the studies. Follow @earthspirit_nature.

Cornell Lab, All About Birds: Arctic Tern

caption:
The Arctic tern (Sterna paradisaea) weighs under 125 g and flies an average of 70,900 km every year.

Eleven terns carried 1.4 g geolocators for the study. South of the Cape Verde Islands their routes split: seven followed the coast of Africa and four crossed the Atlantic to follow the coast of Brazil. The oldest Arctic tern on record was at least 34 years old when it was recaptured in Maine.

Swipe for the numbers. Sources on the last slide.

Source: Egevang et al. (2010), PNAS 107:2078–2081; Cornell Lab of Ornithology.
